You should already be in the computer field, in some capacity or studying something every single night if you're not. There are multiple paths for what you asked as well, even within the two categories below.

InfoSec: You MUST be in the computer field, period. There are all kinds of tards that go out and get their CISSP and complain they can't find a job except for low-paying helpdesk work. You MUST have experience and can actively troubleshoot a lot of items. The two tracks are Application Security and System Security. One is based on development experience (code vulnerabilities), the other is based on hardware and system admin type experience (software/system vulnerabilities). Pick which works for you and head to jobs that give you that experience. Shitty jobs work as you'll learn quickly and can move up as you learn. This path goes more into CISSP and other certs for "overall security". This path is more corporate, dealing with policy, procedure, vulnerability management programs, being the mean guy taking away infected machines, etc. This is the guy you fear walking around in a company, either because they'll hear or see something bad. You also have to have people skills here as you need to get info from people that are usually worried about breaking rules, being fired or worse.

PenTesting: Really, anyone can do this, but this is where the "you have to study if you're not in the field" comes into play. If you want to hack WordPress or phpBB all day - you can, but you have to have PHP and web server experience. Since it's all open source/free, it's easy to start at home, even if you're a plumber with an interest in computers. Once you get into the Enterprise level applications though, you need server experience, database experience and stuff like Active Directory experience. No I'm targeting Windows shops here, cause that's where Enterprise stuff is. Linux is used, but mostly in startups and smaller shops - at least in my personal experience (yes, people are going to argue, that's why I said "in my experience"). This path goes into the OSCP side of things, which I've seen multiple Sr Developers with System Admin experience have problems passing. This is the harder path, but there's more fame this way.

Either way, you learn which things you want to attack or deal with, with experience. There can be money in either method, but it's dependent on how much effort you put into it. I would NOT recommend randomly attacking various companies, even if startups like Voat have developers playing "system admin" and probably do things wrong. That action can land you in jail. There are bug-bounty programs that many corps take part in and set limitations, use those lists to practice.

Source: I'm in InfoSec, have published vulnerabilities under my name and live comfortably. Lots of stress due to the industry, but in the end, it's worth it. As a note: I do not have any certs or college education and I started doing technical support. At my level (PreReq for most jobs is a Masters or PHD, or 15 years exp), certs are kind of worthless unless you want to work for the government or some ass that doesn't realize that you don't have to have a CISSP or OSCP to do a job - I do occasionally explain why I don't have xyz cert and if they don't like it, I shrug it off as "not a fit for me". I typically don't apply to jobs, recruiters find me and I pick and choose where I go.

As a web-dev, you're probably on track for the pentesting side but it's a hard side to go down, IMO. JS and Node are the big ticket things right now, but you need to anticipate the up-coming things as well. Pay attention to all the new stuff coming out, pay attention to all the stupid crap coming out of the NPM packages, as this is one of the worst security areas right now, and publish stuff you find. Look into communities that you can publish security vulns, as posting stuff on Twitter isn't "how to do it".
